claims.text: Depositing CeO2 nanoclusters will enhance low-temperature oxidation activity relative to the unmodified catalyst.
Depositing CeO2 nanoclusters will improve resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO.
Depositing CeO2 nanoclusters will increase catalyst lifetime durability.
The CeO2 modification will not compromise minimal platinum-group-metal usage.
The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy containing catalytic metals such as Cu and Ni with minimal Pd or Pt.
A uniform, thin deposition of CeO2 nanoclusters is the proposed intervention.
The proposed operating domain is simulated automotive exhaust below 150 °C containing H2O and NO, together with accelerated lifetime-representative aging.
CeO2 nanoclusters will locally increase oxygen-vacancy concentration at metal-support interfaces.
The CeO2 layer will facilitate formation and replenishment of active oxygen species at low temperatures.
Improved availability of active oxygen species will lower the oxidation onset temperature for CO and hydrocarbons.
The CeO2 layer will mitigate binding of H2O and NO poisoning species.
Anchoring by CeO2 will reduce nanoparticle sintering and performance degradation during prolonged use.
The modified catalyst will have lower CO and hydrocarbon ignition temperatures than the unmodified catalyst.
The modified catalyst will undergo less degradation after accelerated aging than the unmodified catalyst.
The unmodified catalyst has higher oxidation temperatures, greater vulnerability to H2O and NO poisoning, and greater degradation over time.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on CeO2 loading, dispersion, and interaction with the alloy surface.
